text: Directed, undirected, weighted; adjacency lists and matrices.
a directed graph and its adjacency list

A graph is a set of vertices (points) joined by edges. Edges may be directed (one-way arrows) or undirected, and may carry a weight (a length or a cost). Trees, grids and "who depends on whom" are all graphs.
Store a graph as an adjacency list: vector<int> adj[N] , where adj[u] lists the vertices an edge from u reaches. Memory O(n + m). An undirected edge is stored twice, once in each direction.
Storage Memory Check edge u–v List neighbours of u Use when adjacency matrix g[u][v] O(n²) O(1) O(n) n ≤ about 5000 adjacency list adj[u] O(n + m) O(deg u) O(deg u) almost always
DFS and BFS over adjacency lists; reversing edges.
DFS and BFS from 第14章 work on any graph: replace "the four neighbouring cells" by "every vertex in adj[u] ". A visited array stops the search from going round a cycle forever.

Sorting each adj[u] makes the search visit smaller numbers first, which is what "print in the required order" problems want (P5318). DFS is O(n + m): each vertex is entered once and each edge is looked at once.

"From each vertex, the largest vertex you can reach" is slow from every vertex separately. Turn it around: reverse every edge, then start from n, n − 1, … and label everything each one can reach that has no label yet (P3916).
Graph search can run out of stack on 105-long paths; if that happens, use BFS or an explicit stack instead of recursion.
Kahn's algorithm and recurrences over a DAG.
a topological order: 1 2 3 4 5

A DAG (directed acyclic graph) has directed edges and no cycle. Its vertices can be lined up so every edge points forward: a topological order. Tasks with "must happen before" rules, food chains and course prerequisites are DAGs.

Kahn's algorithm: count each vertex's incoming edges (in-degree); queue every vertex with in-degree 0; pop one, output it, and remove its edges, queuing any vertex whose in-degree drops to 0. If fewer than n vertices come out, the graph has a cycle.

In topological order, every vertex is processed only after all vertices that point into it, so a recurrence over the DAG ("number of ways", "longest time") can be filled in that order, exactly like 第11章(P4017).

Start the topological order from every in-degree-0 vertex, not only from vertex 1: vertices that vertex 1 cannot reach still have to remove their edges, or their targets never reach in-degree 0. Keep "unreachable" as a separate value so it is never extended (P1807).
Chores with durations (P1113) are the same longest-path idea; deciding whether a set of "A < B" facts gives a unique order checks that the queue never holds two vertices at once (P1347).
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. Graph = vertices + edges; directed or undirected; maybe weighted.
2. Adjacency list vector<int> adj[N]: O(n + m); store undirected edges twice.
3. DFS/BFS on graphs: loop over adj[u]; a visited array stops cycles; O(n + m).
4. Sort adj[u] to visit smaller vertices first.
5. "Largest reachable from each": reverse edges, search from n downwards.
6. DAG = directed, no cycle; topological order makes every edge point forward.
7. Kahn: queue in-degree-0 vertices, remove their edges; fewer than n out → cycle.
8. Recurrences over a DAG (count paths, longest path) follow the topological order.
9. Start Kahn from every in-degree-0 vertex; keep "unreachable" separate.
